_readme: Ground truth for the synthesised corpus in disputes/.
Deliberately kept OUT of the dispute records: a label inside the input would be
visible to the agents and would make any accuracy measurement worthless.
expected_outcome is one of: ruled | escalated | human_review.
decisive_rule_ids are the rules a correct ruling must rest on, from docs/policy.md.

cases.rationale: 50% / 3.2 km deviation clears both limbs of RD-1. The rider questioned the route while it was happening and the driver gave no reason RD-2 recognises, so the deviation is unjustified and the fare delta is refunded.
The deviation is material, but the rider asked for the extra stop in the chat and confirmed it on the intake form. RD-2 makes an agreed route change a justified deviation, so the higher fare stands.
6% / 0.3 km is below both limbs of RD-1, so the deviation is immaterial and no remedy arises. The rider's high dispute rate is context only and is not the reason the claim fails (GEN-8).

20% is at the first limb's threshold but 6.5 km independently clears RD-1's gross limb, which exists precisely for long trips where a percentage understates the detour. Unjustified, so the delta is refunded.

The deviation is material and unjustified, but the rider was charged the quoted fixed fare: charged_sgd equals recomputed_estimated_route_sgd. RD-4 says a rider who paid the quoted price was not overcharged. The routing is recorded under GEN-7.

No material deviation, but the breakdown does not sum to the amount charged (breakdown_consistent is false) and the charge exceeds the recomputed fare by the same 3.40. RD-5 refunds a pricing error independent of routing; fare accuracy is the operator's responsibility, not the driver's.

86% duration overrun with a 3% distance variance. RD-6: a trip that took longer without travelling further is a traffic outcome, and the chat shows both parties attributing it to an accident. The time charge stands.

The record has no estimated distance, so route.deviation_km and deviation_pct are both null and RD-1 cannot be tested. EV-1 requires all three inputs; ESC-2 sends it to a human rather than inventing a baseline.

The deviation is material and unjustified and the delta exceeds the SGD 50 autonomous cap, so ESC-4 prepares the ruling as a recommendation but sends it to a human. The merits are clear; the amount is what withholds it.

The driver was 18 m from the booked pickup point and waited 5.5 minutes, so both preconditions in NS-2 and NS-3 are met and the fee was earned. The rider being nearly ready does not unmake a valid charge.

The driver was at the pickup point but waited only 1.5 minutes, short of the 3 minutes NS-2 requires. Under GEN-3 the records must positively support the charge; here they refute it, so the fee is refunded in full.

The driver marked arrival 880 m from the booked pickup point, well beyond the 500 m limit in NS-3, so the wait never started and the fee is invalid however long the clock ran. The pattern is flagged under GEN-7 for the platform's own enforcement.

No arrival was ever recorded and the driver never marked a no-show. Under NS-4 a rider whose driver did not arrive owes nothing, and the fee is refunded. The stationary-and-unresponsive pattern is recorded under GEN-7.

Both parties assert incompatible facts and the driver's position at arrival was never recorded, so NS-3 cannot settle it. The wait alone clears NS-2, which makes the charge arguable rather than proven. NS-6 routes it to ESC-3.
The cancellation came 2 minutes after matching, inside Ryde's published 3-minute free window, and no arrival was recorded. NS-1 makes the fee unchargeable and it is refunded in full.
The driver was 30 m from the pickup point and waited 6 minutes before the rider boarded, and the trip completed. NS-5 makes the waiting fee chargeable on exactly those facts.
Property damage and cleaning are outside the two categories this policy covers. GEN-1 scopes it out and ESC-1 routes it to the support queue with a neutral acknowledgement, without an agent ruling.
